Answer this question from a curated study note: law of the conservation of institutions:

Humans are rule-following.
Environment changes, rules need to change.
But they don't.

Human beings are rule-following animals by nature; they are born to conform to the social norms they see around them, and they entrench those rules with often transcendent meaning and value. When the surrounding environment changes and new challenges arise, there is often a disjunction between existing institutions and present needs. Those institutions are supported by legions of entrenched stakeholders who oppose any fundamental change.

Answer this question from a curated study note: RLM vs. Standard coding agents:

Call rlm_agent() instead REPL instead of separate tool

Both combine LMs with code execution. But in typical agent frameworks, the model calls sub-agents as independent tools. The REPL and the sub-agent are separate. In an RLM, the sub-agent is a function inside the REPL. The parent writes an algorithm, calls rlm_agent() as part of that algorithm, and the results flow back into the program's execution.

The Higgs field is an invisible field that fills all of space.

Some particles interact with it; some don’t.

How The World Became Rich &
Quantifying the Scientific Revolution

Part economics, institutions, and culture

The Scientific Revolution and the Industrial Revolution appear to have been driven primarily by a virtuous cycle of economic development, institutional progress, and cultural change. Rising living standards allowed more people to engage in scientific and innovative pursuits, while also fostering a cultural mindset more open to challenging established ideas. This cultural shift, in turn, supported the development of more inclusive political institutions, which further reinforced economic growth and scientific progress.

Economic Development (40-45%):
The paper provides strong evidence that economic development and rising living standards were crucial factors in driving scientific productivity. Countries with higher GDP per capita and urbanization rates showed significantly higher scientific output. This suggests that having "economic slack" - surplus resources beyond basic survival needs - was critical in allowing individuals to pursue scientific endeavors.

Institutional Factors (25-30%):
The study found a strong association between scientific productivity and inclusive institutions, particularly the activity of parliaments. This aligns with the idea that political freedoms and constraints on government power created an environment conducive to innovation.

Cultural Factors (20-25%):
The paper highlights a shift in attitudes towards innovation, exploration, and challenging authority that occurred alongside rising scientific productivity. This "culture of growth" seems to have been particularly strong in northwestern Europe. The association between scientific output and artistic creativity suggests a broader cultural shift towards innovation.

Education and Knowledge Transmission (5-10%):
While the paper found limited evidence for the direct impact of universities on scientific productivity, the general increase in literacy and education levels likely played a role. However, the study suggests that horizontal transmission of knowledge between countries was less important than previously thought.

Religious Factors (5%):
The study found an association between Protestantism and scientific productivity, though this may be partly explained by economic factors. The impact seems smaller than some historical theories have suggested.

Geographic Factors (0-5%):
While not heavily emphasized in this study, geographic factors like access to trade routes may have indirectly contributed by affecting economic development.

Answer this question from a curated study note: Timeline of Usenet & NNTP:

Usenet starts in 1979-1980 at Duke University and UNC Chapel Hill. The original transport is UUCP (Unix-to-Unix Copy Protocol) — which is literally just a program for copying files between Unix machines over phone lines. One machine dials another, they exchange batches of new articles, hang up. The "protocol" for which articles to exchange was crude — basically send everything and let the receiver discard duplicates.

NNTP arrives in 1986 as a purpose-built replacement that runs over TCP/IP. It doesn't change what Usenet is — the newsgroup structure, the article format, the social conventions all stay the same. It just replaces the transport underneath.

So Usenet is actually a good case study for your framework — the content layer (newsgroups, articles, threading) stayed constant while the transport layer was swapped out underneath it.

Answer this question from a curated study note: When use shift register?

Shift registers are often used for the purpose of saving pins on a microcontroller. Every microcontroller has a limited number of pins for general inputs and outputs (GPIO).

If a project needs needs to control 16 LEDs, that would normally require 16 pins of a microcontroller. In the event that you don't have 16 available I/O pins, this is where the shift register comes in handy. With two shift registers connected in series, we can accomplish the task of controlling the 16 LED's with only using 4 I/O pins. That is quite a difference, and you can save even more pins the more shift registers you have chained together.

Answer this question from a curated study note: list of factors that limit or are complementary to intelligence includes: (5)

IRL speed, data, complexity, humans, physics

Speed of the outside world. Intelligent agents need to operate interactively in the world in order to accomplish things and also to learn8. But the world only moves so fast. Cells and animals run at a fixed speed so experiments on them take a certain amount of time which may be irreducible. The same is true of hardware, materials science, anything involving communicating with people, and even our existing software infrastructure. Furthermore, in science many experiments are often needed in sequence, each learning from or building on the last. All of this means that the speed at which a major project—for example developing a cancer cure—can be completed may have an irreducible minimum that cannot be decreased further even as intelligence continues to increase.

Need for data. Sometimes raw data is lacking and in its absence more intelligence does not help. Today’s particle physicists are very ingenious and have developed a wide range of theories, but lack the data to choose between them because particle accelerator data is so limited. It is not clear that they would do drastically better if they were superintelligent—other than perhaps by speeding up the construction of a bigger accelerator.

Intrinsic complexity. Some things are inherently unpredictable or chaotic and even the most powerful AI cannot predict or untangle them substantially better than a human or a computer today. For example, even incredibly powerful AI could predict only marginally further ahead in a chaotic system (such as the three-body problem) in the general case,9 as compared to today’s humans and computers.

Constraints from humans. Many things cannot be done without breaking laws, harming humans, or messing up society. An aligned AI would not want to do these things (and if we have an unaligned AI, we’re back to talking about risks). Many human societal structures are inefficient or even actively harmful, but are hard to change while respecting constraints like legal requirements on clinical trials, people’s willingness to change their habits, or the behavior of governments. Examples of advances that work well in a technical sense, but whose impact has been substantially reduced by regulations or misplaced fears, include nuclear power, supersonic flight, and even elevators.

Physical laws. This is a starker version of the first point. There are certain physical laws that appear to be unbreakable. It’s not possible to travel faster than light. Pudding does not unstir. Chips can only have so many transistors per square centimeter before they become unreliable. Computation requires a certain minimum energy per bit erased, limiting the density of computation in the world.

Answer this question from a curated study note: Three parts of

"Chapter 16: Computers in the Anthropocene"

(as of June 2024)

1. quantifying digicene/sapiosphere in brainpower (10B vs. 100B, 10B, 1M)
2. Cognitive niches of the pyramid
3. Impacts of those niches being filled by digital intelligence

This chapter aims to show how computers impact society today. First, I’ll show how to understand computers as a technology, by thinking of the total amount of “brainpower” they give us, just as animals and fossil fuels gave us horsepower. A sapiosphere, if you will. There are 10 billion human brains running at 1 petaFLOP. How does digital brainpower stack up? There are 10x more embedded systems (100B), but they run much slower. There are 10B smartphones, but they run 1000x slower than brains. There aren’t many supercomputers, but they do equal human brain speed. All things considered, computers added a bunch of new brainpower to the world, but it’s 1000x less than humans. Still, even without counting AI and GPUs, and even with a slightly slower Moore’s Law, we should expect digital brainpower to exceed human brainpower by 2050.

Then, I’ll show how digital brainpower occupies a different cognitive niche: First, embedded systems buffer the world from disturbances and keep our cars, appliances, and infrastructure running. Second, smartphones, computers, and servers have put everything in a database, which we use for either scrolling feeds, buying goods in marketplaces, or organizing businesses. Third, supercomputers run high-value simulations like finding new deep-sea oil.

What is the result of this new computational fabric in the world? New companies built around databases and screens, job changes due to a massive drop in paper use, digital government surveillance, and a general reliance on our digital symbiotes. Information wants to be free. Information wants to be stored. Electrons want to talk. Electrons want to compute.

Answer this question from a curated study note: Why were Fertile Crescent grains *already* good before human domestication?

Seasonality selects for big seeds

The Fertile Crescent concentrated many already-edible, already-productive annuals with big, non-bitter seeds and short generation times (einkorn/emmer wheat, barley, rye; lentils/peas/chickpeas). Short cycles + big seeds make selection fast and storage easy. The Americas had strong crops (maize, potato, squash), but far fewer regions with dense clusters of large-seeded annuals ready for rapid domestication.

Strong seasonality pre-selects plants that hoard energy in seeds, shatter synchronously, and germinate quickly—traits that humans want. Many American heartlands (e.g., tropics) select different life histories where perennials/tubers dominate; great foods, but often slower to standardize, store, and intensify at scale outside cool/dry highlands.

In Factfulness, Hans Rosling breaks down the global population into 4 levels based on income. The one billion people on Level 1 make $0–$2/day. The three billion people on Level 2 make $2–$8/day. The two billion people on Level 3 make $8–$32/day. And the one billion people on Level 4 make more than $32/day. We can think of the folks who have passed this point as existing on “Level 5: Abundance”. (Or Level 5: Enough.) https://medium.com/@RhysLindmark/a-critique-of-hans-roslings-factfulness-why-we-should-use-5-levels-instead-of-4-dccaac0440b4 This “enoughness” means that you’ve essentially “reached the limit” of Stage 1 Buyer-Seller Positive Sum Games. i.e. You can’t buy/consume/accumulate much more that would actually increase your happiness.
